You use the future perfect for an action completed before another in the future (quand nous aurons fini…) and for suppositions (il aura oublié).
When we’ve finished the cake, we’ll open the presents.
As soon as I’ve sent the invitations, I’ll call you.
In a month, we’ll have left for Paris.
Radu isn’t here? He must have forgotten the time.
By then, everything will be ready.
To form the future perfect: avoir / être in the future + past participle (j’aurai fini, elle sera arrivée).
To use the future perfect after quand, dès que, aussitôt que, une fois que, après que.
To express an action completed at a given moment in the future: “Dans un mois, nous serons partis.”
To make a supposition about the past: “Il aura oublié.” (= he must have forgotten).
To make a step-by-step plan: d’abord… une fois que… d’ici là…

Monday, 4 March 2030. Rose-Hélène turns two. In the evening, after the party, Ioana and Julien sit down in the kitchen with a big calendar and plan the next two months, which will be the busiest of their lives.
Right. She’s finally asleep. She must have eaten too much cake, she was overexcited.
And Radu? He didn’t stay for coffee.
He’ll have gone to Lucia’s. They have to finish the invitations tonight. Right, shall we do the schedule? Otherwise I won’t sleep.
OK. On 29 March, dress rehearsal at La Duchère. On 5 April, departure for Paris. On the 6th, the concert. On the 7th, return.
And as soon as you’re back from Paris, we’ll have to deal with the wedding. My grandmother arrives on 1 May, my parents on the 2nd.
Wait. When your grandmother arrives, will Odile’s flat be ready?
Yes, Odile will have finished repainting the guest room before Easter. She promised me. Well, she said she would have finished it, which isn’t quite the same thing.
And the wedding cake? Sophie said she wanted to start it once we had chosen the flavours.
Radu and Lucia will have chosen them by the end of the week. Lucia wants orange, Radu wants walnuts. Sophie will do both.
Do you realise? In two months it will all be over. We’ll have played in Paris, Radu will have got married, and your grandmother will have gone home by coach.
And how many hours will we have slept?
(laughs) Not many. But when it’s all over, I promise you a week by the sea. Just the three of us.
You said exactly the same thing two years ago. You said that as soon as the hall was inaugurated, we would go on holiday.
And this time I’m writing it on the calendar. Look: “15 May. Sea.” In pen. It can’t be erased any more.

Future perfect = the auxiliary (avoir or être) in the FUTURE + the past participle. Same rules as the passé composé:
English uses “will have finished” too, but French uses it much more, especially after “quand” and “dès que”.
2. After quand, dès que, une fois que
When two actions are in the future and one ends BEFORE the other, the first is in the future perfect:
Once you’re back, we’ll deal with the wedding.
After she has arrived, we’ll go to dinner.

A typical mistake: the present after “quand” with future meaning, as in English (“when I finish”). In French: “quand je TERMINERAI” or “quand j’AURAI TERMINÉ”, never “quand je termine” for the future ✗.
In a month, we’ll (already) have left for Paris.
By the end of the week, they’ll have chosen the flavours.
In two months, it will all be over.
“D’ici là” = by then. “D’ici demain / d’ici lundi / d’ici la fin du mois” = by tomorrow / by Monday / by the end of the month.
Surprise: the future perfect also expresses a SUPPOSITION about something that has already happened:
He isn’t here? He must have forgotten.
Elle aura mangé trop de gâteau.
She must have eaten too much cake.
English has a similar construction: “he’ll have forgotten”, “she’ll have gone home”. Use it as a bridge!
When you report in the past a promise about the future (ch. 38), the future becomes the conditional and the future perfect becomes the past conditional:
Elle a dit qu’elle finirait la chambre.
Elle a dit qu’elle aurait fini avant Pâques.
« Dès que la salle sera inaugurée, nous partirons. »

Ioana had announced a simple party. A cake, candles and the family, nothing more. She had repeated it to everyone for two weeks, like a magic formula. On Monday 4 March, at five in the afternoon, she realised nobody had listened to her. The doorbell wouldn’t stop ringing, and the little flat on rue d’Austerlitz was filling up like a concert hall.

Odile arrived first, of course, since she only had a landing to cross. She was carrying a small cardboard box tied with a red ribbon, and refused to say what was inside. “You’ll see once she’s opened it,” she told Ioana. “Not before.” Then she settled into the best armchair, like a queen awaiting her court.

Sophie came up with a cake she had spent two days making. It was a little chocolate piano, with white sugar keys and, on the lid, two candles shaped like musical notes. “I couldn’t help myself,” she apologised. “I made a piano for your wedding, so now it’s a tradition.”

Karim and Leïla arrived with their daughter, who was now eight and considered Rose-Hélène her personal doll. Mrs Roux came by taxi, with a box of sugared almonds. Théo, who was fifteen and already a head taller than Julien, had brought a score. He had composed a little lullaby for his “goddaughter of the heart”, as he called her.

From Annecy, Pierre and Brigitte had taken the afternoon train, with Manon, who was now studying in Lyon and had gone to pick them up at the station. Pierre carried under his arm a brioche as big as a pillow. “I know,” he said, seeing Ioana’s face. “A simple party. But a brioche is simple. It’s just flour, butter and love.”

Radu and Lucia arrived last, out of breath, their arms full of envelopes. “The invitations,” Radu explained. “We printed a hundred and twenty. As soon as we’ve eaten the cake, we’ll have to go and finish the addresses.” Lucia rolled her eyes. “He’s been saying that since this morning. I say the addresses can wait. A second birthday only happens once.”

At six, Julien set up the computer on the piano. Two windows opened on the screen. In the first was the kitchen in Iași: Elena, Dan and the grandmother, who held the phone too close to her face, so that all you could see was her nose and glasses. In the second was the patio in Seville, with the orange tree, don Manuel and doña Carmen.

So there were three languages and three countries in the same room, and everyone was talking at once. The grandmother sang “Mulți ani trăiască” in Romanian, don Manuel played “Cumpleaños feliz” on the guitar, and Manon struck up “Joyeux anniversaire” in French. The result was a magnificent cacophony. Rose-Hélène, sitting on her father’s lap, clapped without knowing why.

When the moment for the candles came, she blew so hard that she put out both candles and sent a bit of chocolate onto Julien’s shirt. Everyone clapped. In the Iași window, the grandmother shouted something nobody understood, because she had forgotten she had to speak into the microphone and not into the screen.

Before the presents, Théo sat down at the piano to play his lullaby. His hands trembled a little, even though he played in front of hundreds of people at the Conservatoire. The melody was simple, gentle, with something of Henri’s waltz hidden in the last bars. When he had finished, Rose-Hélène held out her arms to him, shouting “Encore!”, which was, according to Ioana, her third word.

In the Seville window, don Manuel applauded by tapping on his guitar. “That boy has gold in his fingers,” he said in Spanish. “When he has finished his studies, let him come to me. I’ll teach him flamenco.” Lucia translated, and Théo turned bright red. His mother, who still worked at the town hall, promised she would think about it. She already knew her son would think of nothing else.

Then came the moment for presents. Rose-Hélène received a little embroidered ie from her grandmother, posted a month earlier for fear it wouldn’t arrive in time. There was also a picture book from Karim and Leïla, red shoes from Brigitte and, from Théo, a little music box that played Henri’s waltz when you turned the handle.

The last present was Odile’s. Rose-Hélène pulled the red ribbon, opened the cardboard box, and took out a small shiny metal object with square holes along one side. She looked at it curiously, then put it in her mouth, like everything she discovered. And a sound came out. A clear sound, a little high, a little sad.

It was a harmonica. Everyone fell silent. Ioana looked at Odile, and Odile nodded, her eyes shining. “It’s Henri’s,” she said softly. “The one in the photo, on the ship. He kept it all his life. Isabelle and I thought it should be used again. And since Rose-Hélène already plays the first three notes of the waltz…”

Julien took the harmonica carefully and examined it. The metal was worn where Henri’s lips had rested for fifty years. On one side, engraved by hand, were two letters, half rubbed away: “H. B.”. He gave it back to his daughter, who blew into it once more, very hard, and burst out laughing.

In the evening, when everyone had left, when Pierre and Brigitte had settled into Odile’s guest room and Radu and Lucia had gone off with their hundred and twenty envelopes, Ioana and Julien sat in the kitchen in front of the big calendar. They planned the next two months. Then Julien wrote, in pen, “15 May. Sea.”

“You know what I’m thinking?” Ioana whispered. “In two months it will all be over. The concert will have taken place, Radu will have got married, my grandmother will have gone home. And in twenty years, Rose-Hélène will open Hélène’s envelope and read the original score of the waltz. And she’ll know how to play it, maybe on the harmonica.” Julien said nothing. He just took her hand.

The following three weeks flew by. Rehearsals now took place twice a week, on Wednesdays and Saturdays. Julien came home late, hoarse from speaking loudly. Ioana was finishing an important project at the office, a school in Vénissieux. And Rose-Hélène woke the whole building at seven every morning with Henri’s harmonica.

Odile, far from complaining, opened her door every morning to hear better. “Henri played out of tune too,” she said. “But he played with conviction. That little one takes after him.” The neighbour on the third floor, a very serious elderly gentleman who worked at the prefecture, protested at first. Then, one morning, Julien caught him on the stairs whistling the three notes.

During those three weeks, Radu and Lucia finished the invitations. They posted them one Sunday evening, all at once, a hundred and twenty envelopes in the yellow box on the street corner. Lucia kissed them one by one before slipping them through the slot, to bring them luck, she said. Radu, for his part, checked three times that he hadn’t forgotten anyone. He still forgot his own boss.

Nathalie found out the next day, at the office, seeing the other colleagues open their envelopes. She said nothing. She just put on Radu’s desk, without a word, a sheet on which she had written: “I suppose my invitation must have got lost in the post.” Radu spent the rest of the day apologising, and brought her the invitation by hand, with croissants from Sophie’s.

The dress rehearsal took place on Saturday 29 March, as planned, in the Hélène Morel hall. Julien had invited the whole neighbourhood, so that the children would get used to playing in front of a real audience. Three hundred chairs had been set out. By six, there wasn’t a single free one left, and people were standing at the back, and even outside, under the lime tree, in front of the open windows.

The children were dressed in black, as they would be in Paris. Inès had a black dress her mother had bought for the occasion, and she kept touching it, for fear it would crease. Yanis wore a white shirt that was too big, lent by his father. Sami had new shoes that hurt him, but he had refused to take them off.

The concert began well. The Brahms dance went by without a mistake. The Spanish tune got half the hall dancing, and Lucia, in the front row, stamped her feet louder than anyone. Then, just as Inès was about to start Henri’s waltz, all the lights went out at once. A power cut across the whole neighbourhood.

There was a cry, then an anxious silence. The children could no longer see their scores. Julien, standing in front of the orchestra, could no longer see the children. Someone switched on their phone torch, then someone else. But before the hall had time to really worry, a note rose in the darkness. A single clarinet note, then a second, then a third.

Inès was playing the waltz by heart. She knew it so well she didn’t need any light. After a few bars, Yanis followed her on the cello, then the violins, one by one, then Sami’s flute. They were all playing from memory, in the dark, listening to each other instead of watching the conductor. And above them, through the big ceiling window, came the last light of the evening.

Julien lowered his arms. There was nothing more for him to do. The children no longer needed him. He turned towards the audience, and in the blue light falling from the roof, he saw the faces: Mrs Mansouri crying, Sami’s father clenching his fists on his knees, Bernard Delorme with his eyes closed, and Odile, in the front row, whistling softly along with them.

When the last note died away, the light came back, as if someone had been waiting for that moment. There was a second of complete silence. Then the whole hall rose as one. The applause lasted so long that the children no longer knew what to do. Some bowed, others laughed, Sami cried, holding his flute to his chest.

After the concert, Marc Delorme came to see Julien, notebook in hand. “Did you plan it?” he asked. “The power cut?” Julien laughed. “No. But I should have. From now on I’ll ask the town hall to cut the power at every concert.” Then he became serious again. “Write that the children played without me. It’s the most beautiful thing a conductor can hear.”

On Friday 4 April, the day before departure, Radu loaded the little van in front of the hall. Yanis’s red cello, the double bass, the percussion, Mihaela’s țambal, carefully wrapped in blankets. He would leave at five in the morning, to reach Paris before noon. Once he had unloaded the instruments at the Philharmonie, he would sleep a few hours at the hostel.

Ioana came with Rose-Hélène to say goodbye. At the last moment, the little one held something out to her uncle. It was her plastic flute, the one she always held upside down. “For Paris,” she said, very seriously, with her two years and her two words. Radu put it between the cello and the țambal, in the best spot in the van.

That night, Julien barely slept. He packed his suitcase three times, checked the tickets four times, and reread the list of sixty children more often than he would have liked to admit. Around two in the morning, Ioana found him in the kitchen, in front of the calendar. “Tomorrow at this time,” he said, “we’ll have arrived. And the day after tomorrow, we’ll have played.”

“And in three days you’ll be back,” Ioana replied, taking his hand. “And you’ll have told me everything. Now go to sleep. A conductor who hasn’t slept plays out of tune.” Julien smiled. It was exactly what Hélène had told him years earlier, on the eve of his first concert with the children. He went to bed, and, for once, fell asleep straight away.
